title: What we find when we’re lost in translation.
author: Murray Sutcliffe
summary: Sutcliffe, a teacher, tells the story of a 2015 bus ride over the Andes when an elderly Chilean passenger tried to explain, through the word terremoto, a number and frantic charades, that a distant earthquake posed no danger. Sutcliffe nodded along without understanding, then spent the journey imagining an apocalypse, only to arrive in a calm Santiago. He uses the episode to amend Wittgenstein's claim that the limits of language are the limits of one's world: often it is the fear of exposing that limit, not the limit itself, that shrinks our world. He connects this to the classroom, where learning depends on the friction between what students can already do and what they are willing to attempt, and where the danger is becoming too good at avoiding that friction. He then asks what is lost when translation apps remove the struggle, and finds the answer in a patient bank clerk in Valencia who met him halfway. The essay concludes that working toward understanding together carries small acts of kindness that frictionless technology can quietly erase.
points: Sutcliffe's pretended comprehension on the bus illustrates how the fear of looking foolish can cut us off from information freely offered.
He refines Wittgenstein by arguing that fear of exposing our limits often shrinks our world more than the limits themselves.
In the classroom, he sees learning as built on the friction between current ability and willingness to risk being wrong.
He warns that avoiding that friction long enough makes the limits of what we attempt look like the limits of what we can do.
Translation technology, he suggests, can remove the patient, halfway meeting that turns communication into kindness.
quotes: He had tried to tell me. I had simply nodded, because admitting that I still didn’t understand felt more uncomfortable than pretending that I did.
But there is something this famous line doesn't quite capture. Sometimes it's not our lack of language that makes our world smaller — it's our fear of exposing that lack.

In these moments, there is a kind of friction: the uncomfortable distance between what we can already do and what we’re willing to attempt. Learning is built upon this friction. Students need to struggle, and they need to get things wrong.
But the most important lesson is not that we learn through friction. It is what happens when we become too good at avoiding it.
Eventually, the limits of what we’re willing to attempt begin to look a lot more like the limits of what we’re capable of.
But if technology can remove some of the friction involved in crossing those boundaries, it’s worth asking: what else do we lose when we remove it?

Technology is very good at making communication more efficient. But I wonder if, in making understanding so frictionless, we occasionally lose the small acts of kindness that were once required to get us there.
